titles: Work From Home Tax Deduction in Canada (Self-Employed)
Your Rent Isn't a Write-Off. Your Office Might Be.
Home Office Deduction for the Self-Employed: The Real Math
yt.description:
Self-employed and working from home? Your rent isn't the write-off. The business share of your home is, if the space qualifies.

The test: the workspace is your main place of business, or it's used only for business and to meet clients regularly. Example: 120 sq ft office in a 1,000 sq ft apartment = 12%. Rent, utilities and insurance of $20,200 × 12% = $2,424 deduction, about $862 of tax and CPP saved in our 2026 Manitoba example ($60K net self-employment income).

Three limits: shared space is cut again by business hours; the claim can't create a business loss (the extra carries forward); and owners should get advice before claiming depreciation (CCA) on the home.

This covers the self-employed only; employees have different rules. Source: CRA, business-use-of-home expenses (canada.ca). Example only; general information, not tax advice.

_vo: Work from home? Your rent isn't a write-off. Your office square feet might be. This is for the self-employed. The space must be your main place of business, or used only for business and to meet clients regularly. Say your apartment is one thousand square feet. Your office room is one hundred and twenty. That's twelve percent. Rent, utilities, insurance: twenty thousand two hundred a year. Twelve percent of that is two thousand, four hundred and twenty-four. That's your deduction. In our sixty-thousand-dollar Manitoba example, that's about eight hundred and sixty dollars of tax and C-P-P saved. Kitchen table? If the space is also personal, you cut the claim again, by the hours it's used for business. And it can't create a business loss. The extra carries forward to next year. Own your home? Claiming depreciation on the office can cost you when you sell. Get advice first. Your home isn't the write-off. Your workspace is.
